query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A multi-tier free‐energy evaluation strategy that combines a sparsely sampled ab initio molecular dynamics (MD) dataset with a machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) and accelerated free-energy sampling (e.g., funnel-based or nested sampling) will compute accurate solid and liquid free energies (including vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions) for multicomponent high‐entropy alloys at a fraction of the computational cost of full ab initio MD or TOR-TILD.
generation.material_initial_state: A representative five-element high-entropy alloy (e.g., a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy) near its melting transition.
generation.intervention: Generate a modest ab initio MD training set across key temperature points for both solid and liquid phases to train an MLIP (e.g., Gaussian approximation or neural network potential) and then use this MLIP together with accelerated sampling techniques to perform thermodynamic integration.
generation.conditions: Temperatures from ambient up to above the melting point (approximately ≤2000 K) in quinary high-entropy systems.
generation.structural_mediator: The MLIP trained on ab initio configurations that embeds key quantum effects (including electron–vibration coupling and anharmonic contributions) governs the accuracy of the free-energy integration across phases.
generation.mechanism: The sparse ab initio MD dataset captures critical electronic and anharmonic interactions while the MLIP provides a computationally efficient interpolation of the potential energy surface; accelerated sampling further reduces the trajectory lengths required to accurately integrate the free energies, preserving fidelity in both phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method should achieve free-energy evaluations with errors within ~2–3 meV/atom relative to explicit ab initio MD, while reducing computational time by roughly an order of magnitude compared to TOR-TILD and full ab initio MD workflows for these systems.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations and TOR-TILD workflows that require extensive sampling in both solid and liquid regimes.
generation.boundary: Initially applicable to well-characterized quinary high-entropy alloys with melting points up to ~2000 K; performance outside this composition and temperature regime is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The accuracy depends critically on the quality and representativeness of the ab initio training set and the transferability of the MLIP. It is uncertain if the method will generalize beyond the initial quinary alloys or capture all electron–vibration coupling effects in more complex chemistries.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a quinary high-entropy alloy (e.g., Al0.1CrCoFeNi), perform full ab initio MD and TOR-TILD free-energy calculations for both solid and liquid phases near the melting point, and independently compute the free energies using the proposed MLIP + accelerated sampling method. Compare the computed free energies and derived thermodynamic observables (e.g., entropy, heat capacity, fusion enthalpy) between the methods.
measurements: Temperature derivative observables such as heat capacity and entropy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the MLIP-accelerated method yields free energies for either phase that deviate by more than ~3 meV/atom from the results of explicit ab initio MD/TOR-TILD calculations, or if derived thermodynamic properties differ significantly, indicating a loss of fidelity in capturing vibrational, anharmonic, or electron–vibration coupling effects.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. decision.trend: Across these studies on multicomponent high-entropy alloys and complex mixtures, first-principles methods have been employed mostly to probe ground-state properties (elastic constants, electronic structures) or to screen compositional spaces for target traits (e.g., high-strength phases). One line of work (PMC11206460, 2020) used ab initio calculations to clarify mechanical behavior in a refractory HEA, while another (PMC8282813, 2021) combined high-throughput computational screening with experiments to identify promising new alloy compositions. More recent research (PMC11375712, 2024) employed electronic structure calculations to map magnetic transitions in a complex alloy. However, these works focused on specific low-temperature or moderate-temperature properties rather than fully resolved free energies across solid–liquid transitions, and none overcame the steep computational cost that arises from including vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling in multicomponent systems. Thus, the core challenge—securing robust, yet tractable free-energy calculations for both solid and liquid phases at high temperature—remains open.
decision.unsolved: No existing published approach balances the required quantum-level fidelity in free-energy evaluations with tractable computational expense for multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their melting transitions. Methods like ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD are highly accurate but scale poorly with the number of constituents and the high temperatures required to capture fusion properties. There is a clear need for a more efficient free-energy sampling scheme that retains full vibrational and anharmonic contributions in complex chemistries.
decision.lever: Adopt a multi-tier strategy combining sparse ab initio molecular-dynamics data with a machine-learning interatomic potential (e.g., Gaussian approximation or neural network potential) to perform thermodynamic integration across both solid and liquid phases from ambient to above the melting temperature. Use a modest ab initio MD training set to incorporate electron–vibration coupling and anharmonic effects. Then employ accelerated sampling methods, such as funnel-based free-energy calculations or nested sampling, to achieve an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational time compared to full ab initio MD or TOR-TILD. Restrict the approach initially to five-element high-entropy systems with melting points up to ~2000 K. To validate, benchmark the predicted solid and liquid free energies and their derivatives (e.g., entropy, heat capacity, fusion enthalpy) against directly computed ab initio MD data on a carefully selected quinary alloy. Discrepancies beyond the target accuracy of ~2–3 meV/atom in free energy would falsify the hypothesis, guiding refinement of the ML potential and sampling strategy.
decision.why: Building an accurate but lean dataset of ab initio MD configurations provides a robust training ground for machine-learning interatomic potentials that embed key quantum effects. Successfully demonstrated for simpler binary or elemental melts, such ML-augmented thermodynamic integration can be extended to high-entropy alloys to preserve the essential vibrational, anharmonic, and electronic contributions at a fraction of the computational expense. By iterating between ab initio reference data and improved potential training, the approach can realistically achieve the fidelity required for fusion and high-temperature property predictions while meeting high-throughput needs.
